themes.theme: Copying Competitors vs. Creating New Vectors

positions.commentary: The speaker mentions Google cannibalizing some of their search to reveal AI as an example of copying a competitor, noting it is adjacent enough but not earth-shattering.
The speaker questions whether McDonald's can successfully rebrand to be a healthy place to go, suggesting it would be a very challenging rebranding to accomplish.
IBM had a great business for a long time with the on-prem server market, but it's going to fade.
Tesla is killing it in the EV market because it's a clean, fresh startup without legacy structures.
GM is not well positioned to go after the EV market because it's a different supply chain and they're not good at software.
The speaker criticizes Altria for investing in marijuana and alcohol, describing these moves as not great and mixed respectively, while suggesting they should have just sold cigarettes.

The speaker suggests that Meta's strategy of copying competitors (like doing reels) is different from McDonald's trying to disrupt its brand (like doing salad), and questions if McDonald's can successfully rebrand as a healthy place.

thesis: This episode argues that legacy companies like Google, Meta, McDonald's, and GM are struggling to adapt to new market vectors (AI, short-form video, EVs) because they are often just copying competitors rather than creating new competition. In contrast, newer entrants like ChatGPT and Tesla are positioned better because they lack the legacy structures that slow down innovation. The core thesis is that successful disruption requires a clean slate or a willingness to cannibalize existing businesses, whereas trying to rebrand a legacy brand (like McDonald's going healthy) is a difficult and often failing strategy.

claims.quote: IBM had a great business for a very long time with the on-prem server market. claims.claim: Tesla is killing it in the EV market because it's a clean, fresh startup without legacy structures.
claims.quote: whereas compared to a clean, fresh startup like Tesla or BYD, they're killing it in the EV market because they don't have all of these legacy sort of business organizational structures and factors weighing them down.

claims.claim: GM is not well positioned to go after the EV market because it's a different supply chain and they're not good at software.
claims.quote: And so all of these other aspects of building an EV car are so different than building an ice car that they're really not that well positioned for it. And if you're thinking of just purely in terms of like discounting their profits over the lifetime, maybe by them going in EV, it extends the lifetime of the company, but it's not necessarily going to be more profits for the investors.

claims.claim: Altria Group has a great business but a bad stock because of their capital allocation.
claims.quote: And I know they're doing a mix of two. I'm just trying to make an example here where ultimately a business doesn't need to exist for forever. And preferences are going to change. Technology is going to change. What you can and can't do is going to change. IBM had a great business for a very long time with the on-prem server market.

claims.claim: The speaker argues that Altria's capital allocation is poor because they are trying to find new markets for a dying cigarette business rather than focusing on selling cigarettes until the market disappears.
claims.quote: Instead, what they did was they said, what's next? Okay, well, let's go and invest in, you know, this new technology. Let's buy huge stake and jewel because that's going to be the next thing. That was a disaster.

claims.claim: The speaker criticizes Altria for investing in marijuana and alcohol, describing these moves as not great and mixed respectively, while suggesting they should have just sold cigarettes.
claims.quote: Let's go ahead and invest in marijuana. That wasn't great for them. Let's go ahead and invest in alcohol. That was, you know, mixed. And so their capital allocation is all over the place because they're trying to figure out what is next for a dying business.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions Chick-fil-A's fried chicken sandwich was really popular, serving as an example of a product that other fast food restaurants copied.
claims.quote: Yeah, so, you know, in the memo, kind of talk about this example with Chick-fil-A and fried chicken sandwiches, where obviously Chick-fil-A's fried chicken sandwich was really popular.

claims.claim: The speaker describes Meta as the best embodiment of the 'civil time' but notes they have failed to create new vectors of competition, copying Snapchat and TikTok before deciding on their future.
claims.quote: Reading this section, I thought that meta was the best embodiment of the civil time, right? They have failed on in pretty much every way to create new vectors of competition. I mean, you know, in our meta discussion, Drew goes through the long list of the apps that never were.

claims.claim: The speaker argues that Meta's decision to focus on short-form videos and content from the internet was smart because the TAM for that is larger than content from friends, even though they lost something in the process.
claims.quote: Now, in their case, though, I would say it was very, very smart because the market or the the tam, if you're thinking of it for just, you know, content that you enjoy is much larger than the tam for just content that your friends share.

claims.claim: The speaker believes one of Mark Zuckerberg's biggest mistakes with Facebook was not allowing more control over who users were sharing with early on, and that he tried to convince people to enjoy handmade content instead of listening to them.
claims.quote: And there's all these discussions at the time that I think personally, one of the biggest mistakes Mark Zuckerberg made with Facebook was that he didn't allow more control over who you were sharing with early on.
